newsitem.title: ABU DHABI: UK minister says no policy change towards Libya.
newsitem.headline: UK minister says no policy change towards Libya.

text.p: British foreign office minister Derek Fatchet said on Wednesday two Libyans charged with a 1988 Lockerbie mid-air bombing should stand trial in Britain.

"I see no progress on the suggestion that those allegedly responsible for the Lockerbie bombing should be tried in a third country," Fatchet said at a news conference in Abu Dhabi, the last leg of a three-country Gulf tour.

Libya has been subject to mandatory U.N. sanctions since 1992, including a ban on international flights and an arms embargo, for failing to extradite two men wanted by Britain and the United States in the 1988 bombing of a Pan Am airliner over Lockerbie, Scotland, which killed 270 people.
Libya had agreed to a trial of the two men in a neutral country, but both the United States and Britain insist the trial must be in their territory.
"I think that it is dangereous, it is a green light to terrorism...I think it is making a suggestion that the British legal system is not principled and fair," he said.

"I think the best way toward is that if the Libyan authorities believe that the evidence is weak against the charges of the Lockerbie offences, they should allow them to come to the U.K. and face a fair trial," he added.

Fatchet, who also visited Oman and Kuwait this week, is the first British minister to visit the Gulf since the Labour government took power last month. He said his tour was to assure Gulf Arab states of Britain's commitment to the region's security.
